tier_reason: Both figures are first-party README statements ('~5x performance uplift for a 1 million generic calls benchmark' vs the stock interpreter; '+0~40% runtime performance in a real world application' vs the BlindMindStudios JIT). The benchmark code is public (tests/abi.cpp 'generic abi benchmark' with tests/scripts/abi.as, nanobench via tests/benchmark.hpp) but no results, CPU, compiler or flags are published, and the 0-40% figure has no published workload at all.

corrections.caveats: Both headline numbers are first-party and thin. The ~5x figure is JIT versus the stock AngelScript interpreter in the same engine (interpreter module built with asEP_INCLUDE_JIT_INSTRUCTIONS false) on a calls-only micro benchmark: tests/abi.cpp 'generic abi benchmark' runs tests/scripts/abi.as benchmark_1M_calls_noarg (a registered generic function that only calls gen->SetReturnDWord(123)) and benchmark_1M_calls_method_arg (SomeClass::add_obj) through nanobench (relative mode, minEpochIterations 5, warmup 1). The speedup comes from angelsea's own generic-call shortcuts (per-function pooling of asCGeneric objects, skipping VM bookkeeping), so it measures call overhead, not general script code; it is not versus the BMS JIT. The repo prints nanobench output but commits no results and states no CPU, compiler or flags; a 'native abi benchmark' and a brainfuck-interpreter benchmark (tests/megatests.cpp) also exist with no published numbers. The +0-40% versus BMS JIT figure is from a private real-world application (King Arthur's Gold dev build) with no published script, data or hardware (README: 'YMMV. If you have results to share, we're interested!'). README says alpha quality and that angelsea may have higher JIT compile times and memory use than the BMS JIT; it depends on a downstream MIR fork (upstream MIR GVN load/store optimisations miscompiled its code). Last commit 2025-09-16, just over 12 months before 2026-10-06, so maintenance is stale.

notes: Record is accurate: README wording, BSD-2-Clause, 31 stars, last commit 2025-09-16 (stale) all confirmed. Shortcomings to record: first-party only, ~5x is versus the plain interpreter on a 1M-call micro benchmark with no published results or hardware, and the 0-40% versus the BMS JIT is an unpublished private-app anecdote; alpha quality.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (nordlow/compiler-benchmark, MIT, 166 stars, public script 'benchmark' with bm_C_using_cuik and gcc_clang_op_flags) shows Cuik ahead of clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.2.1 on check and compile, with the CPU (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350) stated; it falls short of A because the Cuik binary is only labelled '~master' (hard-coded version string, no commit, unknown build compiler and flags). The -O0 cap was considered and does not apply: the metric is compile time, the baseline compilers are release builds, and Cuik's optimizer is also off by default (-O enables it), so both sides run unoptimised codegen.

corrections.caveats: Independent third-party suite, but the gap to tier A is the Cuik build: the script hard-codes its version as '~master' (no commit, no build compiler or flags), and results are from one sample run on one machine (best of 5 per cell). The comparison is at default settings for all three (gcc and clang with no -O flag plus -Wall -Wextra, which they pay for and Cuik does not; Cuik's optimizer is off unless -O is passed, and its check mode -xe is 'type check only', comparable to -fsyntax-only), on one synthetic program shape (long chains of one-line 'return x + ...' functions), so it measures front end plus unoptimised codegen speed only; the 'Run' column (105 us/f for Cuik versus 155 clang and 98 gcc) is of unoptimised output on a synthetic program and says nothing about optimised code quality, which the lead named as a baseline and for which no numbers were found. Timing noise is visible: the suite runs tasks in parallel, one worker pinned per logical CPU (SMT siblings share cores), and the Compile column is larger than the Build column (compile plus link) for every C compiler (Cuik 60.6 vs 57.6, clang 123.3 vs 60.3, gcc 732.5 vs 500.7), so the 1.05x Build win over clang is a tie within noise and the 2x Compile win over clang may be inflated by contention. Numbers are normalised per function while Cuik is capped at 100 x 100 (10,000 functions, 'due to compiler stability limits') against 200 x 200 for the other C compilers, so fixed start-up cost weighs more on Cuik, which if anything understates its speed. The README conclusion ranks Cuik second in build speed after tcc, but its own table shows D's dmd (11.2 us/f) and LuaJIT (4.8) building faster than Cuik (57.6). Cuik's own README says 'unfinished and buggy' and carries no benchmark; a search-result snippet saying its preprocessor is about 2x faster than Clang's was not verified. LLVM as a library (TB versus LLVM backend) is not measured here. Category fit is loose: Cuik is an ahead-of-time C compiler toolchain measured on compile time, filed under jits.

notes: All table numbers (check 6.0/15.4/18.2, compile 60.6/123.3/732.5, build 57.6/60.3/500.7, tcc and cproc rows, Ryzen AI 7 350, Arch Linux, 2026-09) and the derived ratios match the nordlow/compiler-benchmark README; Cuik MIT, 1.3k stars, last commit 2026-07-26 confirmed. Shortcomings: Cuik built from an unpinned '~master', one parallel sample run with visible contention noise (Compile slower than Build for every C compiler), build-speed win over clang is a tie, unoptimised synthetic code only, no optimised code-quality numbers; consider a category override since it is an AOT C compiler rather than a JIT.

tier_reason: The QEMU and FEX comparison is a first-party article by the Box86/Box64 author on box86.org, which is EGRESS_BLOCKED here; a search snippet (news summary of the article) confirms it compared Box against QEMU and FEX on 7-zip and dav1d, but the exact Box86 row numbers in the record could not be re-confirmed. The author's FOSDEM 2021/2022 performance page (rajdakin/box86-fosdem2021-content performances.md) gives first-party Box86 versus native numbers with hardware but no QEMU or FEX rows, no Box86 build flags and no public harness, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Search-result text of the article as recorded by the search agent (not re-confirmed by the verifier; article blocked): 7-Zip MIPS native ARM 6157, Box86 3117 (about 50% of native), FEX 1197 (about 19%), QEMU 691 (about 11%), so Box86 about 4.5x QEMU and about 2.6x FEX (derived from snippet data, article not opened); glmark2 Box86 178 versus native 181. A news summary of the same article (snippet only) gives Box64 at 27-53% of native versus QEMU 5-16% and FEX-emu 13-26% across 7-zip and dav1d. Repo docs/README.md: 'DynaRec ... providing a speed boost between 5 to 10 times faster than only using the interpreter.' First-party FOSDEM 2022 page (Box86 versus native only, 7z 16.02 'Tot' rating): Raspberry Pi 4 5733 native vs 2912 Box86 (51%, 2021), ODroid N2 8981 vs 3811 (42%), Phytium D2000/8 18001 vs 8462 (47%).
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: box86.org is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so the article itself was not opened; the 7-Zip and glmark2 numbers come from search-result text that the verifier could not reproduce, and no CPU model, compiler flags, guest binary versions or QEMU and FEX versions are visible. The measurement is from March 2022 and was made by the Box86 author, a competing project; FEX has changed substantially since (per the catalogued FEX entry, a FEX maintainer said in October 2024 that he had never compared FEX with Box). FEX needs aarch64, so the Box86 versus FEX rows imply an aarch64 machine running an armhf userspace for Box86. The same article's Box64 and Rosetta2 comparison ran on an Apple M1; the machine for the Box86 rows is not visible. QEMU and FEX use softfloat for x87 to keep 80-bit precision while Box uses hardware float (lower precision), which favours Box on x87 code. glmark2 and game rows mostly measure native GL pass-through via wrapped libraries, not the JIT. The author's FOSDEM 2021/2022 page (github.com/rajdakin/box86-fosdem2021-content performances.md) has Box86 versus native only (7-Zip 40-61% of native, dav1d 21-55%, glmark2 96-100%, OpenArena 72-86%) on named boards with 7z 16.02 from Debian, but no Box86 build flags and no QEMU or FEX rows. The 5-10x dynarec claim in the README is versus Box86's own interpreter and has no workload, CPU or flags. The article is also the source used for the catalogued Box64 and FEX entries.

notes: Repo metadata confirmed (MIT, 3.8k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-09-27). Shortcomings: first-party 2022 comparison by a competitor's author, article blocked so the Box86/QEMU/FEX numbers rest on a search snippet the verifier could not reproduce, no hardware or versions visible for those rows; hardware-stated first-party Box86-versus-native numbers exist on the FOSDEM page. Box86 is the 32-bit sibling of the catalogued Box64, not a duplicate.
